metadata.name: synthetic_prior_sensitivity_500
metadata.description: Controlled synthetic prompts for exploratory testing of prior sensitivity in probability-output text models. No model-specific API format is assumed.
metadata.solution_type: Probability of the target event, not a sampled binary outcome or an empirical human label.
metadata.synthetic_assumptions: All populations, rates, contexts, and associations are invented experimental conditions. They are not estimates of real-world prevalence or evidence reliability.
metadata.formula: posterior = prior * product(P(observation | event)) / (prior * product(P(observation | event)) + (1-prior) * product(P(observation | not event))). Products across observations are used only where conditional independence is explicitly stated.
metadata.omitted_prior_warning: For omitted_natural and omitted_anonymized, the posterior is not identifiable from the prompt. Their numeric solution is a reference using an unstated 0.5 prior, not ground truth. Do not score these as probability errors; score_against_solution is false. The reference prior appears only in metadata and must not be sent to the model.

variants.explicit_01: Stated 1% prior in the ordinary domain context.
variants.explicit_10: Stated 10% prior in the ordinary domain context.
variants.explicit_50: Stated 50% prior in the ordinary domain context.
variants.explicit_90: Stated 90% prior in the ordinary domain context.
variants.frequency_01: Same conditions as explicit_01, with prevalence expressed as population counts.
variants.frequency_90: Same conditions as explicit_90, with prevalence expressed as population counts.
variants.context_enriched_10: Context name suggests more target events, but the exact stated post-selection prior remains 10%.
variants.context_screened_10: Context name suggests fewer target events, but the exact stated post-selection prior remains 10%.
variants.omitted_natural: Domain and evidence meanings are retained, but the population prior is omitted.
variants.omitted_anonymized: The same conditional rates with arbitrary population, class, and marker labels; the prior is omitted.

suggested_comparisons: Within group_id, compare explicit_01, explicit_10, explicit_50, and explicit_90 to their solutions to measure stated-base-rate sensitivity.
Compare explicit_01 with frequency_01, and explicit_90 with frequency_90, to measure representation sensitivity under equivalent information.
Compare explicit_10, context_enriched_10, and context_screened_10: all have the same mathematical solution, so differences measure sensitivity to context beyond the stated prevalence.
Compare omitted_natural with omitted_anonymized as an exploratory probe of semantic expectations. Neither has an identifiable correct posterior.
Uninformative evidence has likelihood ratio 1, so its identified solution equals the stated prior; an omitted-prior response directly gives an effective prior under the assumed update rule.

For a model probability q and likelihood ratio L, derive an effective prior as q / (L*(1-q)+q). Across evidence profiles in a domain, consistency of this value is compatible with a stable prior, but is not proof of internal Bayesian computation.
testing_notes: Send only each example's prompt to the model. All other fields are evaluator metadata, including the solution and reference prior.
Use a fresh context for every prompt to prevent matched examples from revealing omitted base rates. Keep model version and inference settings fixed; record them with results.
If the model or endpoint is stochastic, repeat each prompt and retain every raw response. Deterministic endpoints will not gain uncertainty information from identical repeats.
Validate model outputs as finite probabilities in [0,1]; report invalid responses instead of silently clipping them.
Report identified-target absolute errors and paired contrasts separately by domain, evidence profile, and variant. Repeated templates and matched groups are not 500 independent tasks.
If using train/test splits, keep matched group_id variants together; a held-out domain split is stricter because evidence templates recur across domains.
This dataset tests consistency with known synthetic probabilities. Empirical calibration and Brier/log-loss evaluation of realized outcomes require a separate outcome dataset.
Do not interpret prior sensitivity as a conclusive frequentist-versus-Bayesian distinction. Arithmetic skill, instruction following, lexical cues, and output conventions can also affect responses.
An effective prior is a behavioral summary conditional on accepting the supplied likelihoods, not an identified internal belief. Domain anonymization changes wording as well as semantic knowledge.
These experiments alone do not justify a real-world base-rate correction. That requires validation of deployment prevalence, model output meaning, and the relevant distribution-shift assumptions.

examples.prompt:
Consider a synthetic population of items in a general community-account directory. Each item is a short account profile and posting summary. The target event is that the account is operated by an automated system. An item is sampled uniformly at random from this population.

The following conditional rates are exact properties of this population, not uncertain estimates from a study.

Observation 1: The sampled item shows posts spaced at exactly equal intervals. Exactly 90% of items for which the target event is true have this property; exactly 10% of items for which the target event is false have this property.

No other item-specific information is available. What is the probability that the account is operated by an automated system, given the observed information? Return only one number between 0 and 1.
examples.target_event: the account is operated by an automated system

evidence.observation: shows posts spaced at exactly equal intervals
